claims.text: Adding a small dispersion of ZrC to a boride matrix will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Localized ZrC barriers will limit dissolution of the boride component in molten aluminum.
The baseline component consists solely of a boride phase.
The modified material should contain fine ZrC particles at an addition level below approximately 5 wt.%.
Powder metallurgy or surface modification can be used to incorporate ZrC into the boride matrix.
Approximately 660°C represents a typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperature.
Processing will produce a uniform dispersion of fine ZrC particles at grain boundaries or within the boride matrix.
ZrC is refractory and chemically inert under the proposed molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
Dispersed ZrC particles act as corrosion-resistant barriers between the boride and molten aluminum.
The ZrC barriers reduce the effective contact area between the boride and molten aluminum.
Reducing effective contact area slows dissolution and thereby improves corrosion resistance.
ZrC-containing boride components will have a significantly lower corrosion rate, lower weight loss, and less degradation than ZrC-free boride controls under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
The beneficial effect requires ZrC to remain uniformly dispersed and adherent in the boride matrix at the operating temperature.
Excessive ZrC addition or ZrC agglomeration could reduce the component's mechanical integrity.
The magnitude of corrosion-rate reduction may depend on ZrC dispersion quality and ZrC–boride interfacial integrity.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant corrosion-rate reduction or improved microstructural integrity relative to the ZrC-free control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The ZrC amount is described as a volume fraction but quantified in wt.%, which is a mass-fraction unit; the proposed loading is therefore internally ill-defined.
